topics.title: The Cholas: temples, navy and village assemblies

learn.hook: A Tamil king built a temple so tall that its tower dominated the town of Thanjavur, and his son sent a navy across the sea to Southeast Asia!
points: The Chola dynasty rose again in the Kaveri delta when Vijayālaya captured Thanjavur in the 9th century.
Rājarāja I (985–1014 CE) built the great Bṛihadīshvara temple (Rājarājeshvaram) at Thanjavur, completed around 1010 CE.

His son Rājendra I (1014–1044 CE) led an army to the Ganga, took the title Gangaikoṇḍa Chola ('the Chola who brought the Ganga') and built a new capital, Gangaikoṇḍa Cholapuram. He also sent a naval expedition against Shrīvijaya in Southeast Asia.
Inscriptions at Uttaramerur (10th century) describe how members of village assemblies (sabhās) were chosen by drawing names written on palm-leaf tickets from a pot (kuḍavolai).
Chola artists made famous bronze images, such as Shiva as Naṭarāja, the Lord of Dance. The 'Great Living Chola Temples' are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

example.q: The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe choosing assembly members by lot, with rules on who could stand. Why is this interesting for students of government?
steps: Villages managed their own affairs through assemblies.
Members were chosen by a fixed, written procedure, not just by a ruler's order.
This shows an early form of local self-government with rules.
example.answer: It shows that Chola villages had organised local self-government with written rules for choosing members.

learn.reallife: Many classical dancers pose like the Chola bronze Naṭarāja, and copies of it are found in museums around the world.

quiz.q: Who built the Bṛihadīshvara temple at Thanjavur?
quiz.explain: Rājarāja I built it; it was completed around 1010 CE.
quiz.mistake: Confuses father and son

quiz.q: Rājendra I took the title 'Gangaikoṇḍa Chola' after:
options: Building a dam on the Kaveri
His army's expedition to the Ganga region
quiz.explain: The title means 'the Chola who brought (or took) the Ganga'.
quiz.mistake: Does not know where the title came from

quiz.q: Rājendra I sent a naval expedition against:
quiz.explain: The Chola navy sailed against the kingdom of Shrīvijaya.
quiz.mistake: Does not know about Chola sea power

quiz.q: The Uttaramerur inscriptions are about:
options: How village assembly members were chosen
quiz.explain: They describe rules and the lot system for village assemblies.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what the inscriptions record

quiz.q: In the kuḍavolai system, members were chosen by:
options: Drawing palm-leaf tickets with names from a pot
quiz.explain: Names were written on palm leaves, put in a pot and drawn out.
quiz.mistake: Imagines modern voting methods

quiz.q: The Chola bronze Naṭarāja shows Shiva as:
quiz.explain: Naṭarāja means 'king of dancers'.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of Naṭarāja

quiz.q: In which river delta did Chola power rise?
quiz.explain: Thanjavur lies in the fertile Kaveri delta.
quiz.mistake: Places the Cholas in the north

quiz.q: Which Chola king ruled from 985 to 1014 CE?
quiz.explain: Rājarāja I's reign was 985–1014 CE; Rājendra I followed him.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of Chola kings

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know why the Cholas are famous. Tell him!
teach.praise: Huge temples, a strong navy and village assemblies! The Cholas were amazing.
teach.nudge: Good! What did the Cholas build, and how did they reach across the sea?

learn.hook: In 1178, a queen of Gujarat led her army against an invader near Mount Abu and won!
points: In the 11th century, Mahmud of Ghazni (in present-day Afghanistan) raided north India many times, carrying away great wealth. Around 1025–26 he attacked the Somnath temple in Gujarat.
The scholar Al-Bīrūnī came to India in Mahmud's time, learned Sanskrit and wrote the Kitāb-ul-Hind, describing Indian sciences, beliefs and customs.
In the 12th century, Muhammad Ghori attacked. In 1178, Rānī Nāikī Devī of Gujarat, ruling for her young son, defeated him near Mount Abu.
In the First Battle of Tarain (1191), Prithvīrāj Chauhān defeated Ghori. In the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), Ghori won.
After Ghori's death, his general Quṭbuddīn Aibak began to rule from Delhi in 1206, starting the Delhi Sultanate. Many Indian rulers continued to resist in different regions.

example.q: Prithvīrāj Chauhān won at Tarain in 1191 but lost in 1192. What does this show about history?
steps: One battle's result is not the end of the story.
The defeated side may come back stronger after preparing better.
So historians study several events together to understand what changed.
example.answer: That outcomes can change quickly; history must be understood through a series of events, not one.

learn.reallife: Tarain (Taraori) is in present-day Haryana, near Karnal, on the plains north of Delhi.

quiz.q: Which famous temple in Gujarat did Mahmud of Ghazni attack?
quiz.explain: Mahmud attacked the Somnath temple in Gujarat around 1025–26.
quiz.mistake: Picks a southern temple

quiz.q: Who wrote the Kitāb-ul-Hind?
quiz.explain: Al-Bīrūnī studied Sanskrit and wrote about Indian life and science.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the scholar with the ruler he travelled with

quiz.q: Which queen defeated Muhammad Ghori near Mount Abu in 1178?
quiz.explain: Nāikī Devī, ruling Gujarat for her young son, led the victory.
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous queen from a different period

quiz.q: Who won the First Battle of Tarain in 1191?
quiz.explain: Prithvīrāj Chauhān defeated Ghori in 1191.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the results of the two battles

quiz.q: In which year was the Second Battle of Tarain fought?
quiz.explain: The Second Battle of Tarain took place in 1192, a year after the first.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the dates of the two battles

quiz.q: The Delhi Sultanate began in:
quiz.explain: Quṭbuddīn Aibak began to rule from Delhi in 1206.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the start of Mughal rule in 1526

quiz.q: Mahmud of Ghazni came from a kingdom in present-day:
quiz.explain: Ghazni is in present-day Afghanistan.
quiz.mistake: Does not place Ghazni on the map

quiz.q: Why is Al-Bīrūnī's book useful to historians?
options: It is a book of Sanskrit poems
It describes Indian sciences, beliefs and customs of the 11th century
quiz.explain: As a careful observer, he recorded much about Indian society and knowledge.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the value of travellers' accounts

teach.ask: Gappu heard about battles at Tarain. Tell him about the invasions of this period and how Indian rulers resisted.
teach.praise: Raids, battles and brave resistance, and then the Delhi Sultanate. History has many turns!
teach.nudge: Good! Who fought back against Ghori, and what happened at Tarain?

topics.title: New powers, thinkers and links with Southeast Asia

learn.hook: While battles were fought in the north, poets, scholars and temple-builders across India were creating treasures that still shine today.
points: Many regional powers flourished: the Chandelas built the temples of Khajuraho, the Hoysaḷas built richly carved temples at Belur and Halebidu, and the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhar was a famous scholar-king.
Thinkers and reformers: Rāmānujāchārya taught devotion to Vishnu; Basavaṇṇa in Karnataka wrote vachanas (sayings) in Kannada and taught that all people are equal before God.
Literature and science: Jayadeva wrote the Gīta Govinda; Kalhaṇa wrote the Rājataraṅgiṇī, a history of Kashmir; Bhāskarāchārya (Bhāskara II) wrote the mathematics book Līlāvatī.
India's links with Southeast Asia were strong. The Angkor Wat temple in Cambodia, dedicated to Vishnu, was built in the 12th century by King Sūryavarman II.
Despite invasions, Indian cultural practices, learning and temple traditions continued and adapted.

example.q: Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī is a history of the kings of Kashmir written in the 12th century. Why is it special?
steps: Most old Indian texts were poems, prayers or stories.
Kalhaṇa tried to record the history of kings in order and used older records.
So it is one of the earliest works in India written as a history.
example.answer: It is one of the earliest Indian texts that tries to record history in order, using older sources.

learn.reallife: Belur and Halebidu in Karnataka, Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh and Angkor Wat in Cambodia are all UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

quiz.q: The temples of Khajuraho were built by the:
quiz.explain: The Chandela kings built Khajuraho's temples in Madhya Pradesh.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up temple-building dynasties

quiz.q: Belur and Halebidu temples were built by the:
quiz.explain: The Hoysaḷas of Karnataka built these richly carved temples.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up southern dynasties

quiz.q: Who wrote the Rājataraṅgiṇī, a history of Kashmir?
quiz.explain: Kalhaṇa wrote it in the 12th century.
quiz.mistake: Confuses different authors

quiz.q: The Līlāvatī, a book of mathematics, was written by:
quiz.explain: Bhāskarāchārya (Bhāskara II) wrote Līlāvatī in the 12th century.
quiz.mistake: Credits the Gupta-age scientist

quiz.q: Basavaṇṇa wrote his vachanas in:
quiz.explain: Basavaṇṇa's vachanas are short sayings in Kannada.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all religious writing was in Sanskrit

quiz.q: Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu, is in:
quiz.explain: Angkor Wat was built by Sūryavarman II in Cambodia.
quiz.mistake: Places it in a South Asian neighbour

quiz.q: Who wrote the Gīta Govinda?
quiz.explain: Jayadeva's Gīta Govinda is a 12th-century Sanskrit poem.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up poets of different ages

quiz.q: King Bhoja, famous as a scholar-king, belonged to the:
quiz.explain: Bhoja was a Paramāra king of Dhar in Malwa.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the Paramāras

teach.ask: Gappu asks what else was happening in India in the 11th and 12th centuries besides battles.
teach.praise: Temples, thinkers, poets and links to Southeast Asia! Culture kept growing.
teach.nudge: Good! Which great books or temples come from this time?
